scope: Deterministic Java resource release, close-failure semantics, ownership transfer, partial acquisition, borrowed/lazy/asynchronous lifetimes and pooled/shutdown boundaries.

procedure.reusedReadings: Previously read unchanged workflow, complete prompt, wave3 brief, skill-engineering references, comparative research/roadmap and earlier-wave evaluation limits were reused as allowed. Entire assigned package read anew.

corrected.prior: TWR suppression was described as preserving the body's exception without qualifying throwable identity or disabled suppression. The manual factory already had a correct self-suppression guard, but the TWR guidance implied the same protection.
corrected.evidence: JLS21 §14.20.3.1 translates to primary.addSuppressed(closeFailure) without an identity guard. Throwable.addSuppressed rejects the same object even with suppression disabled. Focused runtime controls reproduced that distinction.
corrected.consequence: Reusing the operation throwable in close can replace the consumer-facing primary outcome with IllegalArgumentException; an empty suppressed list can also conceal distinct close failures on suppression-disabled exception types.
corrected.change: Qualify the core suppression rule, explain identity versus disabled recording in the existing routed reference, direct inspection of the actual resource/exception implementation, preserve the existing manual identity guard and require checking release attempts separately from escaping exceptions.

findings.noAdditionalChanges: Ownership, decorator double-close, async termination versus future completion, pooled leases, shutdown escalation and Java 25 preview distinctions already have supported targeted guidance.

filesChangedByReviewer.change: Qualify normal TWR failure preservation and expose the identity/suppression constraints before promising diagnostics.

preservedCapabilities: Acquire/release ownership, explicit borrowing and transfer; returning a view alone does not transfer ownership.

Closeable versus AutoCloseable contracts and narrow declared exceptions; interruption/partial-release limits.
Files streams versus borrowed BufferedReader.lines, terminal consumption versus close and iterator ownership.
Async ownership follows actual-use termination, not just exposed-future completion; private cleanup/rejection/cancellation considerations.
Executor and Java 25 StructuredTaskScope lifecycle contracts, lease versus physical connection, bounded admission and shutdown ordering.
No implicit toolchain upgrade, preview enablement, dependencies or generalized cleanup framework.
replacedCapabilities: The unqualified claim that TWR always records cleanup failures and preserves the body's throwable was replaced by the actual conditional contract.
